summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek; Ivan Saika-Voivod; Styliani Consta
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the spatial distribution of sodium ions (Na+) within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets using molecular dynamics simulations and an analytical reference model. The authors demonstrate that unlike at room temperature where ion distribution is nearly uniform, supercooled droplets (200 K) exhibit a heterogeneous solvent structure characterized by a low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core and a high-density, disordered subsurface. This structural inversion drives the expulsion of Na+ ions from the core to the subsurface region. The paper introduces the concept of 'electrostatic confinement,' a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, which dominates at room temperature but is overridden by solvent density effects at supercooling. The findings have significant implications for understanding atmospheric aerosol reactivity, electrospray ionization in mass spectrometry, and the preservation of macromolecular conformations in low-temperature environments.

Executive Summary
This study investigates the spatial distribution of sodium ions (Na+) within supercooled aqueous nanodroplets using molecular dynamics simulations and an analytical reference model. The authors demonstrate that unlike at room temperature where ion distribution is nearly uniform, supercooled droplets (200 K) exhibit a heterogeneous solvent structure characterized by a low-density, tetrahedrally ordered core and a high-density, disordered subsurface. This structural inversion drives the expulsion of Na+ ions from the core to the subsurface region. The paper introduces the concept of 'electrostatic confinement,' a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, which dominates at room temperature but is overridden by solvent density effects at supercooling. The findings have significant implications for understanding atmospheric aerosol reactivity, electrospray ionization in mass spectrometry, and the preservation of macromolecular conformations in low-temperature environments.

Research Context
Ion distribution in droplets dictates chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols. Supercooled clusters are notoriously challenging to equilibrate compared to room temperature systems. Previous studies of supercooled clusters were limited to sizes ≤ 100 molecules, precluding core formation. Recent work revealed an anomalous inverted radial density profile in pure water clusters at low temperature. It remains unknown if this low-density core differentiates ion distribution from room temperature.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines single and multiple ions in supercooled aqueous mesoscopic clusters. We hypothesize that the low density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution. The hypothesis could not be explored earlier because small cluster sizes precluded the low density core. We introduce a reference analytical model to determine forces determining a single ion's location. The model predicts the ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's COM. We name this effect 'electrostatic confinement' and present conditions under which it is evident.

Methodological Details
Simulations were performed using molecular dynamics implemented in GROMACS v4.6.1. Water molecules were modeled with the TIP4P/2005 transferable intermolecular potential model. Na+ ions utilized OPLS-AA parameters with a charge of +1 e. Systems were simulated at T = 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K representing standard and supercooled conditions. Each nanodroplet was placed in a periodic cubic box of length L to avoid periodic image interactions. The length of cutoff for Coulomb and Lennard-Jones interactions was set at L/2. Simulations were carried out in the canonical ensemble with constant N, V, and T. Temperature was controlled using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with a time constant of 0.1 ps. Equations of motion were integrated with the leap-frog algorithm using a time step of 2 fs. For N = 776, ion densities converged after 400 ns for simulations starting from surface and center. For N = 1100, equilibration time was assumed longer by a factor of τ 1100 /τ 776 ≈ 2. Structural analysis included Voronoi volumes, tetrahedral order parameter q T (r), and distance to fifth neighbor d 5.

Procedures And Architectures
The energy of the charged droplet is written as the sum of the electrostatic energy and surface energy. The energy related to the distance of the ion from the droplet's COM is given by a harmonic potential. The spring constant K(ε) depends on the relative dielectric constant of the solvent. The maximum of the coefficient K(ε) is attained at ε = 1 + √ 3 ≈ 2.73. The expectation value of the square of the distance of the ion from the center of mass is estimated. The EC is more pronounced when the ion is localized at the center of the droplet. The effect will be more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius and intermediate dielectric constant. Sampling requires simulation times much longer than the diffusion time Dt sim R 2. Typical simulation times are in the 10 ns to 100 ns range at T = 300K. The model predicts the ion is always subject to a force toward the droplet COM.

Key Results
At high T, ρ(r) is characterized by a flat curve in the interior decaying sigmoidally at the interface. At low T, there is significant layering and an increase in density as r increases towards the surface. At high T, ρ N a (r) is approximately constant in the interior and decays within the subsurface. At low T, the peak of ρ N a (r) is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in ρ v (r). The single Na + ion tends to reside in the highest density environment at low T. For N = 100 at low T, ρ N a (r) is peaked just below 0.3 nm despite constant ρ v (r). Multiple ions at T = 200 K are expelled from the drop's core and show a maximum at the subsurface. For 776 H 2 O molecules at T = 300 K, the distribution decays as 0.42 exp(-(1.14 -x)/1.2). For 1100 H 2 O molecules at T = 200 K, two peaks are observed at 0.52 nm and 1.5 nm. The lower intensity peak at 0.52 nm corresponds to one ion exchanging with ions giving the outer peak.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The heterogeneous radial density at low T drives ions to the disordered subsurface. The dielectric constant increases with increasing density, favoring ion location in denser regions. Electrostatic confinement dominates at room temperature but is overridden by solvent density at supercooling. The low density core expels ions, a phenomenon not predicted by the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation. The analytical model serves as a reference for comparing with simulation data. These findings assist in interpreting ion mobility-mass spectrometry data on macromolecule conformations.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model predictions may deviate from simulated distributions when the low density core affects ion location. For N = 100, the cluster is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations than larger droplets. The cluster of N = 100 does not show a tetrahedrally organized core. The value of λ P B is interpreted qualitatively due to significant shape fluctuations in droplets up to a few thousand molecules. The increase in q T (r) beyond 1.6 nm is not indicative of increased tetrahedral order. The study assumes all charge is in the surface for the Poisson-Boltzmann reference model.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Two simulations were run for N = 360 and 776 to ensure equilibration after adding a single Na + ion. For N = 776, ion densities converged after 400 ns for simulations starting from surface and center. The appearance of two peaks for multiple ions does not indicate a metastable state.
